#7715. I Thought Multi-Tools Were a Gimmick — Then I Took One on a Camping Trip

If, like me, you think multi-tools are gimmicky gadgets, you might change your mind once you discover how handy they are when your toolbox isn’t within reach.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

I admit I scoffed when my partner first started raving about his Leatherman Wave+ multi-tool. I thought it looked like an expensive, over-elaborate gadget that was destined to gather dust in a junk drawer.

However, as a keen hiker and camper, I’ve discovered how useful it is to have pliers, knives, a saw, scissors, files and other tools packed into one compact, quality piece of kit. I’ve also watched my tech-obsessed partner regularly reach for its precision tools when tinkering with his electrical equipment.

Ahead, I’ll share how a tool I once dismissed as a gimmick earned a permanent spot in my pack, and what two experts think makes a Leatherman worth the price tag.

I had to realize that our Leatherman Wave+ isn’t meant to replace a well-stocked toolbox to understand its value. Instead, it fills the gap when dedicated tools aren’t conveniently available or really needed.

At home, I regularly use the tool’s tiny scissors to carefully prune dead leaves from our many houseplants, the knife to open packages and the small screwdriver to tighten the legs on my glasses. My partner is an IT professional who also has an impressive collection of synthesizers, and he regularly reaches for the tool to make small technical repairs and splice wires.

I’ve found the Wave+ even more useful when we’re borrowing my parents’ campervan, hiking, or camping. The bottle opener is handy for those after-adventure beers, the serrated knife slices baguettes for trailside sandwiches, the saw cuts small, dry branches for kindling, and the screwdriver has adjusted our portable stove and tightened folding chairs.

The pocket-sized multi-tool packs 18 functions into a stainless-steel form that measures just four inches when closed and weighs 8.5 ounces. Alongside the tools I’ve mentioned, it has pliers, bit drivers, a wire stripper and crimper, a ruler, an extra knife blade and file, and an admittedly slightly-tricky-to-use can opener.

While I don’t regularly use all 18 tools, and I might never use some, having the selection provides peace of mind, especially in remote places.

Daniel Kilburn, founder of Emergency Action Planning and a preparedness expert, has carried his Leatherman Surge since his military service in 2006. “It’s an expedient tool to have on hand when you know you’re going to be someplace where you won’t have access to any others,” he says.

Scott Emanuel of knives, multi-tools, and outdoor equipment retailer Heinnie Haynes is also a multi-tool convert. He appreciated having one for quick fixes while renovating his cottage, and particularly rates the needle-nose pliers, which rival standard models rather than acting as an emergency substitute.

Kilburn suggests multi-tools can be a useful starting point for someone who doesn’t own a toolbox, and at the other end of the spectrum are the tinkerers and prepared problem-solvers Emanuel sees as natural fits.

“The person who will value a Leatherman is the one who spends their after-hours in the garage building stuff that they probably never need, it’s the kind of self-reliant and prepared person who you rely on to solve a problem,” Emanuel says.

The Leatherman Wave+ currently costs $129.95, meaning it should be a well-considered purchase rather than an impulse buy.

It’s reassuring to know that you’ll be investing in a refined product designed because of a genuine practical need. Founder Tim Leatherman conceived a pliers-based multi-tool after encountering car and plumbing problems while traveling through Europe in the 1970s, and after careful development, he launched the original Pocket Survival Tool in 1983.

Today you’re paying for that established reputation and durable construction, and Leatherman backs its products with a 25-year warranty.

“They’re ridiculously well built, really well regarded, and their choice of tools is good,” Emanuel says. He describes sought-after Leathermans as the “collectible top end of the multi-tool market.”

Kilburn recalls seeing lower-priced multi-tools failing his comrades during their military career. “Some disintegrate over time because they were just cheaply made with poor-quality material [and] poor-quality steel,” he says. His Leatherman Surge, meanwhile, has lasted over 20 years. If replacing it again, he says he would choose Leatherman over his backup Gerber multi-tool because he prefers its feel and durability.

Leatherman makes a wide range of multi-tools, so it pays to consider which functions you’ll genuinely use. The Signal model adds outdoor-focused features suited to camping, including a ferrocerium rod, emergency whistle and sharpener, but omits scissors. I use scissors enough for plant pruning, first aid and gear repairs that the Wave+ remains the better fit for me.

If you’re unlikely to use most of its functions, a smaller, cheaper multi-tool could make more sense. The Wave+ is also heavier than minimalist models, and there’s a learning curve when figuring out where everything lives.

Don’t forget that a premium multi-tool only represents good value if you look after it. We remove dirt after outdoor adventures and dry and lubricate it before storing. We also avoid forcing it to tackle jobs better suited to full-size tools. I wouldn’t, for example, choose its compact saw over a dedicated full-size version for pruning substantial tree branches in my yard.

If you’re using a Wave+ in the UK, like me, be aware of the country’s knife laws. You need a “good reason” to carry it in public because its blades lock. However, Emanuel explains that the legal language is ambiguous, so you shouldn’t assume you can carry one wherever you go just because it’s part of a multi-tool.

The Wave+ has convinced me that a good multi-tool is more than merely an expensive gimmick. It may not replace dedicated tools, but having so many functions at my fingertips in a form that is so compact, portable and easy to use makes it a practical, worthwhile investment.

The Wave Plus is a multi-tool workhorse. It packs 18 tools in one, including sharp blades, spring scissors, wire cutters, and more.

#7713. Indirectly Inciting "Followers to Flood" Business "with False Reviews, Calls, and Emails" May Be Tortious

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Couture v. Noshirvan, decided Tuesday by Judge Kyle Dudek (M.D. Fla.):

[T]he story begins with a viral video of a parking-lot argument. Convinced that one of the women [Couture] had broken the law, Noshirvan set out to uncover her identity. He deployed a "sock puppet" social media account, posing as a concerned bystander to gain her trust. The ruse worked, and Couture unwittingly confirmed her involvement. Armed with that info, Noshirvan published a TikTok video broadcasting both Couture's name and her employer—Garramone Plastic Surgery.

Noshirvan's followers quickly took to the comments with ideas for how to retaliate. One suggested to "schedule appointments and not show up[.]" Another pitched calling Garramone Plastic Surgery to ask about Couture. And two users went so far as to agree that "we are now working on reviews for his business[.]" Just as the comments suggested, Garramone Plastic Surgery received emails, voicemails, and fictitious reviews….

Apparently having endured enough of this negative publicity, patients cancelled their scheduled procedures, a physician left the practice, and Garramone Plastic Surgery hired security personnel and installed an enhanced security system. Garramone Plastic Surgery now seeks to recover those damages….

The court held that Garramone's tortious interference claim against Noshirvan could go forward:

To succeed on a claim for tortious interference under Florida law, the plaintiff must prove: "(1) the existence of a business relationship, not necessarily evidence[d] by an enforceable contract; (2) knowledge of the relationship on the part of the defendant; (3) an intentional and unjustified interference with the relationship by the defendant; and (4) damage[s.]" …

There is no shortage of evidence showing both protected business relationships and Noshirvan's knowledge of them. Garramone Plastic Surgery's testimony highlights interference with its existing patients and with Dr. Allison Yee, an associate physician who left the practice amid the fallout. Florida law does not require Noshirvan to know these individuals by name. He merely had to know the business relationships existed. The targeted nature of the online attack—especially the bogus reviews planted on the Yelp and Google pages—is more than enough for a jury to infer that Noshirvan knew he was interfering with the practice's clientele.

Further, there is evidence of competent damages. Garramone Plastic Surgery testified that it lost about $900,000 in non-surgical procedures and $130,000 in surgical procedures. Then there are the costs Garramone Plastic Surgery incurred for security personnel and a security surveillance system. …

What is not clear though, is whether there was intentional, unjustified interference…. But Noshirvan's intent in making his posts is best left for the jury. A reasonable jury could conclude Noshirvan's intent was to harass and target Garramone Plastic Surgery. [Plaintiff's theory is that] {Noshirvan incited his followers to flood Garramone Plastic Surgery with false reviews, calls, and emails.} … A reasonable jury could also conclude, however, that Noshirvan's intent was just to harass and target Couture.

The court also concluded that Noshirvan couldn't use 47 U.S.C. § 230 to avoid liability:

Section 230 protects a "provider or user of an interactive computer service" from being treated as the "publisher or speaker" of information provided by another. While there is admittedly little case law regarding users of interactive computer services, a user or provider is still responsible for their own encouragement of, or material contribution to, unlawful content. See, e.g., Elliott v. Donegan (E.D.N.Y. 2022); Doe #1 v. MG Freesites, LTD (N.D. Ala. 2022). Noshirvan published multiple videos on his social media accounts specifically identifying Garramone Plastic Surgery. The videos can be interpreted as a call to action for his followers—especially given Noshirvan's comments that he had done this to numerous people before. Noshirvan cannot escape liability by focusing on the reviews, calls, and emails. After all, it is his own publication that a reasonable jury could conclude sparked them….

But the court concluded that, though Garramone's incitement theory might support a tortious interference claim, it couldn't support a civil conspiracy claim, which requires enough evidence of an "agreement" to do something unlawful:

An agreement can be express or implied. But where a party lacks direct evidence of a conspiracy, circumstantial evidence only establishes an agreement where it "outweighs all reasonable inferences to the contrary."

Garramone Plastic Surgery cannot show an agreement exists…. Garramone Plastic Surgery … claims direct incitement, but the evidence falls short. Noshirvan certainly gave his audience the practice's name, but he did not issue the marching orders to attack its reviews. That call to action came from someone else—a user named @motherofrockets. Garramone Plastic Surgery does provide a post where Noshirvan suggested calling businesses around the practice. But that post is a far cry from launching a targeted harassment campaign against Garramone Plastic Surgery, which is the conduct at issue. There is simply not enough evidence for a jury to conclude Noshirvan directed his followers' actions.

Garramone Plastic Surgery separately leans on indirect incitement, claiming that alone is enough to prove a conspiracy. But that argument expands Florida civil conspiracy liability beyond its breaking point…. When courts find an actionable agreement, there is often at least some direct communication between the conspirators. That crucial link is missing here….

The record here certainly shows that Noshirvan's followers committed wrongful acts. It may even show that he knew his followers were bound to respond with this sort of misconduct. But the Court declines to endorse a rule that anticipating bad behavior creates a conspiracy, at least not without some Florida law in support.

In conducting its own research, the Court could find only one case involving social media. See Conradis v. Buonocore (M.D. Fla. 2021). It offers no meaningful support to Garramone Plastic Surgery because the defendant directly encouraged and recruited third parties to engage in a specific act. At bottom, Garramone Plastic Surgery has failed to prove an actionable agreement between Noshirvan and his followers….

UPDATE 11/11/26 12:19 pm: Note that plaintiff alleges that Noshirvan created the videos because someone paid him money to do that, not out of political or moral conviction; but this particular opinion did not seem to turn on this distinction.

#7712. American Woman Convicted of Receiving Military Training from ISIS in Syria

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today, a federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Halima Salman, 27, a U.S. citizen and former resident of Brooklyn, also known as “Umm Khattab al-Muhajir,” of receiving military-type training from the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS), a designated foreign terrorist organization, in Syria. Salman was convicted after a two-week trial before U.S. District Judge Natasha C. Merle.

“The atrocities committed by ISIS, including mass executions, sexual slavery, and the systematic terrorizing of civilian populations, represent some of the gravest crimes of our time,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “There is simply no excuse for aligning with or receiving military training from an organization responsible for such suffering. Today's verdict sends a clear message that those who support this death cult will be found and prosecuted.”

“With today’s verdict, Salman is held accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “ISIS ravaged Syria and caused havoc across the globe; our Office will continue to prosecute those who supported its murderous reign.”

“It’s been nearly a decade since Halima Salman sought military training from ISIS in Syria, and today justice has been served,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI remains unwavering in its vigilance. We will continue to identify, disrupt, and bring to justice those who support foreign terrorist organizations and threaten the safety of our nation and our communities.”

As proven at trial, in September and October 2016, Salman’s parents traveled with her and her eight siblings out of the United States, ultimately destined for ISIS-controlled territory in Syria.

In late 2016 or early 2017, Salman was 18 years old and married to an ISIS fighter in Syria, where she voluntarily sought military-type training and received authorization to carry ammunition and an assault rifle from ISIS. Salman received a document certifying that she successfully completed that training, a copy of which was found on her husband’s cellphone after it was recovered from the battlefield. Also on her husband’s device were photos depicting Salman with an ISIS flag in the background and a video that shows her brandishing an AK-47 rifle.

The case was investigated by the FBI New York Field Office. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs provided significant assistance obtaining evidence overseas.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Adam Amir and Amanda Shami for the Eastern District of New York are prosecuting the case, with valuable assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Reich, Paralegal Specialist Emily Woodruff and Trial Attorney Patrick Cashman of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

#7711. 8 Reasons a Contractor Might Give You an Outrageously High Estimate

If you just got a quote for a home repair that made your eyes water, there's probably a reason it's so high. A team of contractors weighs in with possible explanations.

If you just got a quote from a contractor that was way more than you thought it would be, join the club…it happens to the best of us. In fact, it’s a pretty common occurrence. Sometimes, though, the quote is so high that you can feel your mouth forming words you shouldn’t be saying. As someone who has been on both sides of such interactions, I can say that contractors don’t like them any more than you do. They know you can shop around, and they need your business. So what’s the deal with ridiculously high quotes?

I didn’t find any shortage of contractors willing to weigh in on this topic — one that is near and dear to their professional hearts. If a quote just made you hyperventilate, take a deep breath and check out some of the possible reasons why it’s so much higher than you expected.

“If an HVAC unit has a defective part that needs replacement, most of my clients will immediately ask how much the replacement part costs,” says HVAC technician Tamer Sayed. “I always tell the current market price and the misunderstanding often starts here. A few clients forget to take into account the labor and consultation fees. They assume they only had to pay for the replacement part.”

The same thing can happen with plumbing and electrical jobs. The part needed to get things working again may be small and inexpensive, and it may only account for a small portion of the quote. Sometimes the labor quote seems excessive, and that’s usually because the client doesn’t understand what’s involved with the repair.

Jake Vincett, a builder from the UK, makes this observation: “A lot of the time, the customer is comparing quotes for different work, because the cheaper one has included a surface repair whereas the more expensive one has quoted for fixing the underlying problem…It’s common that the customer doesn’t know or consider the amount of work going into a project. A new driveway isn’t just laying tarmac – it’s digging out the old one, laying the sub base, etc.”

Plumbing, electrical and HVAC expert Bob Cardwell adds: “It’s often not only one problem to fix but a bunch of small fixes. Even though it might be possible to fix the original problem without addressing the additional issues, an experienced and reliable technician will not ignore them, will try to fix them and will discuss them with the homeowner.”

Failing to provide a quote that addresses underlying issues and then delivering a sky-high bill at the end doesn’t just make the customer unhappy, says HVAC and plumbing expert Ryan Osterkamp. “It can make them feel like we don’t know what we’re doing.”

Osterkamp is used to hearing customers say: “I can go get that part for $X at Home Depot.” What they aren’t thinking about is the amount of training and expertise that made it possible for our technician to quickly and accurately diagnose the issue, have the supplies they need in their truck and be able to do the repair same day. Sure, you may save money by going with the guy on Facebook that works out of an old, unlabeled truck, but if his work doesn’t hold up, will he fix it without giving you the runaround? Is he insured? Does he offer a warranty?”

Tariffs, inflation and the economy in general are pushing prices up, and the dollar has lost a lot of its purchasing power for the average American. The same is true for contractors. “The fact of the matter is, we’re working harder now and making less,” says remodeling contractor Kevin Cullen. “In today’s economy, a lot of people are chasing the price to the bottom and shopping for the cheapest number. Unfortunately, they usually get what they pay for.”

A contractor who knows problems might creep up, such as a rotten subfloor that needs replacement during a toilet repair, makes an effort to warn customers as part of the quote. Potential problems aren’t always obvious. “There are times,” says Nika Tveretinova, who operates an HVAC business in Sacramento, “when the actual fix isn’t that complicated, but it’s the access that makes things tough—especially with equipment installed in an attic or cramped quarters. Sometimes we also find an old installation that needs a safety or code correction before we can put everything back together.”

In such situations, a higher-than-expected quote that you can reject is far better than a higher-than-expected bill you have to pay because the work is already completed.

Joshua Kurz founded NumeralQ, a home improvement pricing guide, and he cautions against comparing a bid you receive from a contractor to information you find online. “Owners often find an estimate online, and rather than waiting for a bid, they assume that number will be the actual cost. These estimates are helpful when determining a budget, but they are not interchangeable for actual bids. A 1,500 sq ft roof in one market will not necessarily cost the same in another market, and bids can even differ for neighboring houses.”

If you find a guy on Facebook who charges a low price to do a repair, there’s no guarantee that the repair will last or be up to code. When that person makes a mistake, a licensed contractor working on the same system at a later date might have to fix it, especially when inspectors are involved.

“Over a 40-year career,” says Cullen, “I’ve found many surprises: unsupported headers, no king or jack studs, undersized headers, poorly installed headers that aren’t flush and have gaps, termite damage, carpenter ant damage, water damage, mold. That’s not every job, but you never know when a homeowner bought a house in which a Rube Goldberg did the work on it.”

Sometimes a house is in such poor condition that a small repair, such as stopping a plumbing leak, can turn into a major project that involves replacing pipes, walls or subfloors. Rather than simply declining the repair, some contractors will offer a ridiculously high quote to avoid falling into a sinkhole of extra work. If the customer accepts the quote, the contractor won’t lose money by taking the job. A customer who rejects a bid can keep shopping with no harm done.

#7710. Why Not Seek the Win/Win?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"Why not seek the win/win?" Justice Brett Kavanaugh posed that question to Colorado's attorney during last week's oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a case involving Catholic preschools and the state's nondiscrimination requirements. His question raises a broader issue: Why is compromise so difficult in conflicts between religious freedom and LGBTQ rights?

Some background: Colorado operates a universal preschool program that provides public funding for children attending participating schools, including religious schools. But participating schools must agree not to discriminate on several grounds, including sexual orientation and gender identity. Catholic preschools argue that these requirements interfere with their religious mission, which includes teaching Catholic doctrine about marriage and requiring families to support that teaching. Colorado maintains that religious schools may participate, but must comply with the same nondiscrimination requirements as other schools.

During oral argument, Kavanaugh noted that approximately 2,000 preschools participate in Colorado's program, while only 34 Catholic preschools are involved in the dispute. The record does not identify any family headed by a same-sex couple that has sought admission for a child to one of these schools and been rejected. Why couldn't Colorado accommodate these schools while ensuring that other families had ample preschool options?

Colorado's attorney responded that equal access to publicly funded education requires more than the availability of alternative schools. The Catholic schools have a principled position as well. Why should they have to compromise their religious identity to participate in a generally available public program? They aren't asking Colorado to endorse Catholic doctrine, only to permit them to maintain their religious mission.

So why is compromise so elusive? St Mary illustrates a dynamic I wrote about in an article several years ago on Masterpiece Cakeshop, another Colorado religious freedom controversy. I argued that conflicts over religious freedom and LGBTQ rights reflect profound cultural divisions in American society. These controversies implicate competing understandings of identity, dignity, and equality.

For traditional religious believers, marriage and sexuality implicate fundamental religious convictions. Requiring religious schools to disregard those convictions in their admissions policies seems like an intrusion on religious autonomy. For supporters of LGBTQ rights, allowing publicly funded schools to exclude children because of their parents' relationships seems like a denial of equal dignity and citizenship. Each side regards the other's position as demanding a concession on something fundamental. Besides, each side may think it has compromised enough. Colorado doesn't prohibit religious instruction in funded schools; the schools don't ask Colorado to endorse their position on same-sex marriage.

This isn't the first time the Court has confronted such a problem. About a decade ago in Zubik v. Burwell, Justice Elena Kagan explored possible accommodations in a contraception mandate controversy, and the Court subsequently sought additional briefing on a compromise.

Kavanaugh's question makes practical sense. The difficulty is that the parties don't understand the controversy primarily in practical terms. Each sees fundamental principles at stake. The Court will resolve the legal dispute in St. Mary. But it cannot resolve the deeper social divisions that make compromises in these cases so difficult.

I discuss these questions in a new episode of Legal Spirits, available here.

NEXT: Indirectly Inciting "Followers to Flood" Business "with False Reviews, Calls, and Emails" May Be Tortious

Mark Movsesian is the Frederick A. Whitney Professor of Contract Law and the Director of the Center for Law and Religion at St. John's University School of Law. He writes and teaches in law and religion, contracts and international and comparative law.

#7708. What Those Little Holes in Your Plug Prongs Are Actually For

Those little holes in electrical plug prongs have a purpose, but it isn't what most people think. Here's why they're still there.

Not all electronic cords look the same. Some have two prongs; others have three or even four. Some have prongs at weird angles, or are even designed for orange electrical outlets. Odds are most people have also seen electrical prongs with holes in them, but the reason for them isn’t common knowledge.

Those two tiny circles often appear near the ends of the metal blades, and newer outlets no longer depend on them. Learn how the feature started, why some manufacturers still use them, what homeowners should know about plug safety, and more.

The holes originally helped keep plugs from slipping out of outlets. Some older outlets had small bumps inside that fit into the holes when someone plugged something in. That changed when Underwriters Laboratories began requiring outlets to hold plugs securely without those bumps.

“Most manufacturers stopped putting the detent nibs on the female contacts, as it made it much harder to meet the maximum force to withdraw and did nothing for the minimum requirement, as the gage had no holes,” according to the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA).

Basically, the bumps made plugs harder to remove, so manufacturers stopped using them. Today, outlets grip the prongs instead. If a plug starts slipping out, the outlet may need to be replaced. The holes aren’t a child safety feature, either. Tamper-resistant outlets use built-in shutters to keep children from sticking objects inside.

“TRRs work like normal outlets,” according to the Electrical Safety Foundation International. “When you plug into a TRR for the first time, you may be able to feel the internal shutter system engaging. If excessive force is needed to insert a plug into a TRR, there’s a chance that the plug, not the receptacle, is damaged.”

Manufacturers sometimes use the holes to hold the metal prongs in place while making plugs. They don’t help electricity flow through the plug, though. The holes can also hold small safety tags or locks on unplugged appliances. However, these shouldn’t replace proper safety equipment. OSHA also has rules for preventing equipment from accidentally starting during certain types of workplace maintenance.

The holes aren’t even required under American electrical plug standards. Manufacturers can make plugs without them, although NEMA has rules for their size and placement when included. They also have nothing to do with grounding. On a three-prong plug, the round prong handles that job. The two flat prongs work the same way whether they have holes or not.

#7707. School Board Can Order High School Teacher to Remove "Hate Has No Home Here" Rainbow Poster

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From McIntyre v. Little Miami School Dist., decided Monday by Judge Matthew McFarland (S.D. Ohio) (appeal pending):

Plaintiff George McIntyre is a teacher at Little Miami High School, a school within Defendant Little Miami School District ("District"), where he teaches American History and Advanced Placement European History. McIntyre placed a poster in his classroom displaying the slogan "Hate Has No Home Here" ("Poster"), depicted below:

As shown above, the Poster features five hands holding hearts filled with distinct symbols, including the American flag, a peace sign, the rainbow pride flag, and the transgender pride flag. McIntyre hung up the Poster to remind his students to "treat all their classmates with mutual respect, regardless of personal opinions or beliefs." …

The District's "longstanding practice" has been to permit teachers to decorate their classrooms and display personal items. That latitude, however, is "defined by" the District's Little Miami School Board ("Board") policy.

That policy landscape shifted when the Ohio General Assembly enacted House Bill 8, known as the Ohio Parents' Bill of Rights. That statute requires school districts to provide parental notice and review for materials containing "sexuality content" and allows parents to opt out for alternative assignments. "[S]exuality content" is defined as "oral or written instruction, presentation, image, or description of sexual concepts or gender ideology in a classroom setting," but explicitly excludes "[i]ncidental references to sexual concepts or gender ideology occurring outside of formal instruction or presentations on such topics." On October 28, 2025, the Board adopted Board Policy 5780.01, incorporating the statute's definitions and notice/opt-out requirements into District policy.

The Board considered restricting classroom wall-hangings exclusively to the U.S. flag, the Ohio flag, and school-related displays, but ultimately concluded that state law and Board Policy 5780.01 provided sufficient oversight. Under District guidance, concerns that a classroom display contains "sexuality content" under state law or Board Policy 5780.01 are subject to a three-tiered review: first by the school principal, then on appeal to the superintendent, and finally to the Board….

In September 2025, Defendant David Wallace, the Board President, visited McIntyre's classroom and photographed the Poster. Thereafter, Wallace contacted District Superintendent Regina Morgan, requesting that McIntyre remove the Poster. Morgan relayed the request to Little Miami High School's Principal, Kevin Harleman.

Harleman spoke with McIntyre about the Poster, and asked whether McIntyre tied the display to his curriculum or classroom discussions, or if it was simply a decorative wall hanging. On February 2, 2026, McIntyre emailed Harleman, identifying specific content standards within the model curriculum for his classes that he felt the Poster was "especially applicable" to. McIntyre further noted that, while the Poster applied to those broad historical themes, it was not used as a formal instructional device and instead was "a reminder that [his students] must treat their classmates with mutual respect." Harleman forwarded that email to Morgan.

The next day, Morgan informed Wallace that, upon her review, while the Poster contained sexual identity symbols, she did not "believe a reasonable observer would conclude its primary purpose [was] to prompt discussion, provide instruction, or solicit student engagement on sexual concepts or gender ideology." Under the "display guidelines," Morgan acknowledged that it was "now a Board decision as to how to move forward." …

[On February 25, t]he Board voted 4 to 1 to classify the Poster as sexuality content under Board Policy 5780.01 and ordered its immediate removal from McIntyre's classroom….

The court rejected McIntyre's claim that the Board's actions violated his First Amendment rights:

Although public employees "undoubtably enjoy certain rights," those rights "do not transform them into 'sovereigns unto themselves.'" Rather, "the government, just like a private employer, retains 'control over what the employer itself has commissioned or created': the employee's job." That authority carries particular significance in the context of public education, where Ohio's compulsory-attendance requirements give public school teachers "a captive audience for their in-class speech." …

[Thus], the Sixth Circuit has held that a public school teacher's in-class curricular and pedagogical choices are not protected by the First Amendment. In reaching this holding, the Sixth Circuit reasoned that "[w]hen a teacher teaches, the school system does not regulate that speech as much as it hires that speech. Expression is a teacher's stock in trade, the commodity [ ]he sells to [his] employer in exchange for a salary." Since Ohio law left curriculum choices to elected school boards as "an accountability measure," those boards are entitled to "regulate the content of what is or is not expressed" on their behalf….

Here, McIntyre spoke as a public employee pursuant to his official duties when displaying the Poster in his classroom. McIntyre hung the Poster to foster a respectful environment among his students and later identified specific state curriculum standards that he believed the Poster supported…. McIntyre's motivations and actions were directly related to, and arose from his professional responsibilities as a teacher shaping his students' learning environment.

Whether McIntyre used the Poster for formal instruction is immaterial. He gained access to and control over the classroom wall space through his position as a public school employee, not as a private citizen. His ability to maintain classroom displays thus existed within the scope of that public employment, which the Board regulated through established policies. As McIntyre displayed the Poster pursuant to his official duties, his expression constituted unprotected employee speech.

Contrary to McIntyre's argument, the Supreme Court's holding in Kennedy v. Bremerton School Dist. (2022) does not alter this conclusion. Unlike the high school coach in Kennedy, who offered a brief prayer while essentially "off the clock" after a game, McIntyre maintained a permanent display on his classroom wall that was visible during school hours. Managing the classroom environment during the school day relates to his job responsibilities, not private citizen speech. Kennedy thus does not compel a finding that McIntyre spoke as a private citizen…. The Board was [thus] entitled to restrain [McIntyre's] speech, and McIntyre is not entitled to declaratory judgment that his First Amendment rights were violated….

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7706. Elon Musk Is Pulling the Plug on Cybertrucks to Focus on Something New

Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production next year as Elon Musk shifts attention to its Cybercab. Here's what the change means.

Tesla Cybertrucks have dominated headlines even before they hit the road. But now it appears their time in the automotive world spotlight might be coming to an end. The company’s CEO Elon Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory to make room for the Cybercab, the company’s self-driving taxi.

Learn why the company is changing direction and what the news means for the Cybertruck.

Austin American-Statesman/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images

In a Nov. 6 post on X, Musk wrote, “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

Tesla began delivering Cybertrucks in late 2023, but sales haven’t lived up to expectations. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates published by Cox Automotive, U.S. sales fell by nearly half in 2025. The truck has also faced criticism for its price, design, and quality issues, as well as several safety recalls.

Current owners can continue driving their Cybertrucks, and existing warranty terms still apply. Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill also addressed concerns about future repairs. “Tesla will maintain spare parts and service will continue support,” he wrote on X on November 6. He didn’t specify how long that support would last.

For anyone still waiting on a Cybertruck, the news is less encouraging. In a Nov. 9 post on X, Musk wrote, “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”

Tesla hasn’t said which customers will receive their trucks or how it plans to handle the remaining orders.

The Cybercab is Tesla’s two-seat electric car designed to drive itself. It doesn’t have a steering wheel or pedals because it won’t need a human driver. Tesla has already started offering Cybercab rides in parts of Austin. The company plans to expand the service, although the vehicles aren’t widely available yet.

Musk denies that Tesla is ending production because the Cybertruck isn’t profitable. He says the company can put its Texas factory to better use by making Cybercabs.

#7705. The Best Air Quality Monitors of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Glenda Taylor, Additional research provided by Tiffany Lewis

Published Nov 15, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Indoor air quality monitors can help you breathe easier at home by detecting hazards you can’t see or smell. Gases like radon and carbon monoxide are colorless and odorless but dangerous if inhaled, and these home devices may also identify other pollutants, including volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and airborne particulate matter like dust and pollen. They can serve as a first alert, signaling when to leave an area where the air is unsafe or prompting you to start clearing pollutants and head off health problems. Keep in mind, however, that not all air quality monitors detect all harmful pollutants.

Concerned about the dangers of hidden pollutants lingering in the air of typical homes, we decided to test a number of today’s most popular air quality monitors. We began by extensively researching more than 40 air quality monitors to narrow the field and then selected a range of models to test. (Spoiler: Not all of the air quality monitors we tested earned a spot on this lineup.)

It’s easy to take steps to improve the air quality in your home with an air quality monitor. The best air quality monitor will depend on which pollutants you want to keep track of and whether you prefer a basic or tech-forward model. Our favorite is the Airthings 292 Wave Mini Indoor Air Quality Monitor. It monitors total VOCs (TVOCs), radon, temperature, humidity, mold risk, and outdoor pollen levels. It also comes with smart-home capability and easy-to-use air quality indicators, and it’s suitable for multi-room use.

Ahead, find out what the devices can do and see how the models listed below fared in our hands-on testing to help you choose the best air quality monitor for your home.

Bottom line: Choosing the right air quality monitor depends on specific needs, from detecting VOCs to integrating with smart-home systems.

When it comes to air quality monitors, accuracy is essential. While we didn’t have access to a laboratory for testing, we could offer a measure of control by testing all the monitors under similar situations to see if the readings would correspond when compared to one another. The following monitors all detected the presence of pollutants in our hands-on tests, and we would not hesitate to recommend any of them to help our readers choose a product to detect airborne pollutants in the home.

To measure chemical pollutants in the air without spending a lot, consider the well-priced Wave Mini. The Wave Mini detects TVOCs, humidity, and temperature in the room. After spending a few hours exposed to a dish of oil-based stain in a closed box, the monitor’s TVOC levels spiked. When we compared its temperature and humidity readings to other monitors being tested, the readings were comparable. We believe it accurately portrayed all three readings.

The Wave Mini offers visual indication of air quality in the room, which is accessible when the user waves a hand in front of the monitor. A light flashes green for “healthy,” yellow for “caution,” and red for “poor” air quality.

Users can purchase a hub separately, allowing them to integrate with smart-home products such as Google Assistant and Alexa. The Wave Mini also tracks outdoor pollen levels via the app that syncs with a local weather service. If users don’t have a specific need for monitoring carbon monoxide, radon, or dust, the Wave Mini may be just the right budget-friendly device to keep track of chemical pollutants in the home.

Get the Airthings 292 air quality monitor at Amazon.

Amazon, increasingly offering more of its own brand of products, has entered the air quality monitor field with this device, which measures particulate matter, TVOCs, carbon monoxide, humidity, and temperature. It’s ideal for bedrooms because the small white cube with a little stainless steel vent in front doesn’t have a large display that might keep some folks awake. Instead, a tiny indicator light at the top that shines green, yellow, or red notifies the user of the current air quality. We didn’t find the indicator light to be bright enough to be annoying; it was just bright enough to display the air quality at a glance. However, it only works in a darkened room—it’s not bright enough to see it in sunny daylight.

The Amazon smart air quality monitor syncs with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, and we found it simple to connect to both. We were unable, however, to connect the monitor to our Echo Show (not included), although it’s advertised as being able to do so. We’re not sure what caused the glitch, since our Echo Show and the monitor individually synced with the Alexa app, but it’s possible it will only connect with newer models of the Echo Show (ours is an older model). Still, the Alexa app on our smartphone provided excellent real-time readings and charts that made it easy to see the air quality.

We tested this monitor in our test box for VOCs and particulate matter. For the first test, we put a dish of oil-based stain in the box, gave it a couple of hours to infiltrate the air, and then checked the app. The VOC reading had spiked. We then opened the box to check the monitor—the indicator light shone red (hazardous air quality). For the second test, we shook the dust mop over the box and monitored the app on our phone. The PM2.5 reading spiked in about 5 minutes and fell 20 minutes later as the dust settled.

To test the CO sensor, we put the monitor in the garage, started the car, and closed the doors. We watched on our smartphone as the CO reading on the app rose. When we opened the garage door, the indicator light was red. We brought the monitor out into the fresh air, and the light turned green in about 10 minutes.

Compared with the other monitors we tested, the Amazon smart air quality monitor’s temperature and humidity readings were right on target. Overall, we liked this little monitor, and we felt it was accurate and discreet enough not to detract from bedroom or nursery decor.

Get the Amazon air quality monitor at Amazon.

This monitor was quite an overachiever in our testing! It connects using Bluetooth technology via the Airthings app and provided detailed reports about our home’s air quality. It will also connect to smart-home devices, such as Alexa, but not via Wi-Fi. Instead, users must download the IFTTT app for their smartphone, which allows a connection between Wave Plus and Alexa.

The first test we performed on the Wave Plus was in a friend’s home where radon was previously detected and is being treated. They have a professional radon detector, so we wanted to see if the Wave Plus would also detect the gas. We positioned it in the basement of the home and left it there for a week.

On our return, we checked the Airthings app and found a radon reading of 3.5pCi/L. This was the exact reading the professional radon detector was showing. When we waved a hand in front of the Wave Plus, it flashed a yellow light that told us the air quality was affected but not hazardous. When we took the Wave Plus outside in the fresh air, the radon level dropped, and the light turned green to indicate healthy air.

We then tested the Wave Plus in our test box where we exposed it for 2 hours to a dish of oil-based stain, a product that contains VOCs. When we checked the monitor, the light was red (indicating hazardous air quality), and on the app we saw that the TVOC reading had spiked. We also compared the monitor’s temperature and humidity readings to those of the other monitors, which were consistent.

We performed one more test—a very unscientific CO2 test. We know that smoke contains CO2, so we took the Wave Plus to the garage and put it on a bench. We used our beehive smoker to blow little puffs of smoke directly on the monitor. The CO2 levels on the app increased slightly, and the indicator light turned yellow. We felt it was detecting some CO2, but we couldn’t tell if it was sensing as much as it should have been. Still, it registered an increase similar to the CO2 detectors on other monitors, so we felt the smoke from the beehive smoker didn’t contain much carbon dioxide.

Get the Airthings 2950 air quality monitor at Amazon or The Home Depot.

The AirVisual Pro air quality monitor by IQAir boasts advanced laser technology, airflow control, and a crafted calibration algorithm to detect precise particulate matter and CO2 data. We felt the most important readings on this monitor for allergy sufferers were the PM1, PM2.5, and PM10 readings. These sensors detect various-size airborne particles, ranging from pollen, which is rather large and can be detected by the PM10 sensor, all the way down to ultrafine dust that can’t be seen but is easily inhaled.

The AirVisual Pro syncs with smart-home systems using either Wi-Fi or IFTTT. We tested both, and both worked well. The best thing about this monitor is its large visual display screen. It’s nice to be able to check the app, but in our opinion, it’s even better to see a visual display at a glance without having to use a smartphone first. Another plus: This monitor gathers outside air quality ratings via local weather reports and displays them prominently.

When we put the AirVisual monitor in our test box and shook a dust mop over it, all three PM sensor readings spiked, which indicated that it was detecting a range of particulate matter sizes. After 30 minutes, the PM10 and PM2.5 readings dropped, as we suspected they would, because the dust had settled. However, the PM1 reading only declined slightly, which we think was due to the extra-tiny particulates that remained airborne longer. The PM1 reading didn’t drop for another hour.

The air quality monitor also detectsCO2 levels, temperature, and humidity. We tested the CO2 sensor by putting the monitor in the garage and blowing puffs of smoke on it from our beehive smoker. The CO2 readings increased slightly, but they didn’t spike. Still, that was consistent with our other monitor tests for CO2.

This specific monitor had some trouble with temperature and humidity, as both readings were off by more than 7 degrees Fahrenheit/points compared to the other monitors. Also, it doesn’t detect VOCs. Overall, this is a handy monitor to detect the presence of primary allergy triggers, such as airborne particulates.

Get the IQAir air quality monitor at Amazon or Walmart.

Those looking for a portable air quality monitor to detect pollen and other airborne particulate matter may find the Temtop P600 air quality monitor to be just the ticket. It uses a Quantum Semiconductor International (QSI) laser diode to detect particulate matter as small as 2.5 microns. A highly sensitive diode also found in professional laboratory equipment, it also detects larger particulates, such as pollen, in the 10-micron range.

The unit has a kickstand that folds out, so users can stand the monitor on a table, nightstand, or even a tent floor when camping out. The first thing we did was charge it fully using the included USB cord, then we started testing.

There wasn’t too much to test on this one, however, since the P600 detects only airborne particulate matter. We put it in our test box and shook a dust mop over it. This monitor doesn’t sync with smart devices, so we couldn’t monitor the readings remotely from a smartphone. Instead, we checked it every few minutes to see if it had changed. The readings predictably spiked after 10 minutes and then gradually dropped (after about 25 minutes) as the dust settled.

One of the upsides to this Temtop model is that it displays air quality over 12 hours on a chart readout. This helped us see air quality changes over the course of a day. Unfortunately, the battery runs down pretty quickly—we had to charge it every morning for a couple of hours in order for it to run the rest of the day. The alternative is to leave it plugged into the USB cord, but the cord plugs into the bottom of the monitor so it won’t sit upright when plugged in. As a solution, we recommend turning the monitor on periodically to check the air quality in a room and then turning it back off to save battery life.

Get the Temtop P600 air quality monitor at Amazon.

Before we chose monitors for hands-on testing, we researched more than 40 models, looking for various sensor types and paying close attention to buyers’ reviews and ratings. We also reached out to an industry expert to get some additional insight. Lisa Townley, the associate director of product management/replacement parts at Carrier, a global provider of HVAC solutions, says, “As people are focused on the health of their indoor environments more than ever before, it’s imperative that they take steps to improve their living and working spaces, including the air they breathe.” She goes on to say that knowing what’s in your air is important because you can “take steps to lower the likelihood of mold … better manage allergens and asthma triggers … and create conditions for improved sleep.” She adds that air monitors with advanced technology to detect finer particles down to 2.5 microns or smaller are particularly useful in the home. We took this expert advice into consideration when choosing which products to test.

For our actual tests—and we must say right off the bat that these were not scientifically controlled trials—we created situations we felt mimicked (or exceeded) real-life air quality problems. To test whether monitors with particulate matter (PM) sensors worked, we put them in a large box and shook a very dirty dust mop over the top. We then monitored the PM readouts on smartphones (or manually) to see when or if they spiked and when they fell (as the dust settled).

We used wood stain, which contains VOCs, including formaldehyde, to test the monitors with VOC sensors. We placed an open dish of oil-based wood stain in the test box and allowed the fumes to infiltrate the box for a couple of hours before checking the readings.

We got a little more creative when testing other sensors! We tested monitors with carbon dioxide (CO2) sensors by blowing puffs of smoke directly on the monitors using our beehive smoker. We tested for carbon monoxide (CO) by putting the monitors with CO detectors in a closed garage with a car running inside. We tested a single monitor to see if it would detect nitrogen dioxide (NO2) by starting a wood fire in the fireplace of our she shed and then closing the flue and monitoring the readout on our smartphone.

To see how well radon sensors worked, we tested them in the basement of a friend’s home, where we already knew radon was an issue.

Temperature and humidity were casually tested by comparing those numbers with other monitors and using the average of the readings (minus the highest and lowest, which we threw out) to determine consistency.

We looked for readout increases and decreases but didn’t compare actual numbers. The detection numbers varied from monitor to monitor from the start, and we felt that one monitor might receive more exposure to a pollutant than another, even though we tried to keep the exposure levels similar. If the readings more than doubled, we deemed it a “spike.”

We also examined and analyzed how easy it was to sync the monitors with Bluetooth; Wi-Fi; or If This, Then That (IFTTT) capability.

To arrive at our awards, we gave models points using a rubric—the better we felt the monitor performed during a test, the more points it received. At the end of testing, we added the points and used them to determine the best category for each monitor.

The monitors we tested ranged from single-pollutant sensors, such as simple radon detectors, to multiple-pollutant detection models that tracked the e humidity levels and several toxic gases. In most cases, a consumer will want a monitor that detects the type of air pollution that puts their home and family at the most significant risk.

For example, consumers who live in a region with known radon problems will want to look for a radon detector or a carbon monoxide detector if they’re concerned about automobile exhaust fumes seeping in from an attached garage. In addition, the following factors are important considerations for consumers shopping for an air quality monitor.

Consumer-quality monitors are not as precise as laboratory detectors, but they’re typically good enough to alert household members that airborne particulates and toxic gases are present.

Monitors that detect dangerous gases, such as VOCs and carbon monoxide, feature electrochemical sensors that react to the presence of gaseous toxins in the air. In some monitors, these sensors must be manually calibrated, but many of the newer models are precalibrated.

Monitors designed to detect dust, allergens, and other airborne particulates do so by estimating the amount of particulate matter that passes in front of a laser. Though valuable, these measurements may not be exact for two main reasons: larger PM might not drift into the laser chamber, and the laser might overlook the tiniest PM.

Home air quality monitors can detect a range of pollutants and will generally detect one or more of the following. Some may detect additional contaminants, but these are the most common.

While some air quality monitors are relatively straightforward, others are pretty high-tech. For example, some models are Wi-Fi capable, and others connect to smartphones and devices via Bluetooth capability or IFTTT technology. Such monitors come with apps that can be downloaded to a smartphone, and then the app walks users through the installation process.

Single-pollutant detectors, such as carbon monoxide detectors, are among the simplest to use because they often just plug into an outlet. If they detect the gas in question, they emit a high-pitched alarm. The best air quality monitor for any individual should be easy to use, depending on the person’s technical skill level. Consumers will want to avoid choosing a complex model with a huge learning curve that requires watching online videos for hours just to figure out how it operates.

Most air quality monitors are relatively small devices, with a sensor unit and a screen that displays how much of the pollutant is currently in the air. Portable units, which fit in a tool belt, purse, or tool bag, are the smallest of all. These are well suited for testing the air on jobsites or in rental homes that don’t have stationary monitors.

Many monitors have the ability to detect numerous problem gases and pollutants and are suitable for multiple spaces. Those who want air quality monitoring to integrate with smart-home technology—so it can display information on a phone or respond to voice commands—will want to look for a smart air quality monitor.

Some people prefer visual alerts rather than numbers or charts that can be challenging to decipher. Today’s monitors often provide color-coded lights that indicate air quality at a glance. Typically, a green light indicates good air quality, a yellow light signifies the air quality is less than optimal but not dangerous, and a red light is a warning that the air quality is poor.

Response time refers to how quickly an air quality monitor will sense the problem and alert the household. Higher-quality devices often have quicker response times because their sensors are more accurate. Response times will also vary depending on which pollutant the monitor is tracking.

For example, some carbon monoxide monitors will sound an alarm after detecting a low level of gas over a few hours; however, if they detect a higher level, the monitor will sound the alarm after just a few minutes. Monitors that measure dust and pollen may not emit a warning at all but simply track and record the varying levels of the pollutants by the hour.

Air quality monitors are either corded (running on electricity from a standard household outlet) or battery-operated (powered by rechargeable batteries). Both are efficient, but for those who need to test air quality in a storage shed or another remote location, a battery-operated model is the handiest.

Very few things are as important as the quality of the air your family is breathing. If you’re new to air quality monitors, you likely have some questions.

According to SmartAir, a developer of air filtration products, the accuracy of air quality readings on monitors falls between 70 percent and 85 percent. While most monitors are as accurate as possible, no single model is 100 percent accurate.

The most common pollutants are airborne particulate matter, such as dust, pet dander, and pollen. However, some other airborne irritants to be aware of are carbon monoxide, lead, radon, and carbon dioxide.

A few simple ideas can improve poor air quality:Clean regularlyKeep your home well ventilatedPurchase an air purifierMaintain your heating and cooling systemsAdd house plantsClean air ductsClean regularlyKeep your home well ventilatedPurchase an air purifierMaintain your heating and cooling systemsAdd house plantsClean air ducts

They sense high or unhealthy levels of particulate matter or toxic gases and alert residents if the levels become dangerous. Many options on the market rely on color-coded air quality indicators to alert users as to the status of the air quality.

Most consumer models can’t detect mold. However, consumers can purchase a home mold test with a petri dish and ingredients that will trigger mold growth if the home has a mold problem. While growing mold may seem counterproductive, it allows consumers to discover whether mold spores are present in the air, so they can take steps to locate the source of the mold and get rid of it.

#7704. The President Nominates Circuit Judges, Not Senators

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Circuit seats belong to the circuit, and not to the state.

There has been a momentous shift in the relationship between the President and the Senate, and most people have missed it.

Let's start with the Eighth Circuit. The Trump Administration interviewed Justice Cody Hiland, but determined he was not up to the task of being a circuit judge, so they offered him a federal district court seat as a consolation prize. Hiland shot back at the White House Counsel and refused the seat. He even wanted to rub it in Trump's face. The White House made a stellar nomination with Judge Lee Rudofsky. Hiland then told an entire room of law students about his experience as a lesson that should be learned. But Hiland had a friend in a high place. Senator Boozman of Arkansas lobbied Senator Tillis of North Carolina and Senator Cornyn of Texas to block Judge Rudofsky.

Apparently there were some discussions between the President and Boozman, and the President folded. Maybe Trump determined that he needed as many judges confirmed before January, so the identity of the judge didn't matter. Maybe Trump didn't want to create more problems with his caucus. Maybe Trump just didn't care. Who knows? Trump withdrew Rudofsky and nominated Hiland. There is no guarantee that Hiland gets a hearing and makes it through the process. We are so late in the game. And frankly, I wouldn't blame some of the other conservative senators from the Eighth Circuit for putting Hiland through the paces at the hearing. It's not clear to me he'll be able to answer all the questions. But regardless of what happens, Senator Boozman won and President Trump lost.

Now, onto my home, the Fifth Circuit. It is painfully clear there was some sort of deal between Judge Southwick and Senator Wicker. In no universe would the White House have picked Todd Butler without that deal. I've yet to hear anyone provide me a single shred of evidence that he is conservative beyond saying "All southern lawyers are conservative. Plus he's a Christian." What about Nathan Johnson and James Talarico? Moreover, Southwick announced on September 29 that he would take Senior Status, making it virtually impossible for another nominee to be selected.

Yesterday, I watched Butler's confirmation hearing with interest. He received a few softballs from Senator Grassley, a very warm welcome from Senator Kennedy, and some surprisingly nice questions from Senator Booker about representing police officers. Butler did not seem to understand departmentalism and mis-cited Marbury v. Madison. His answers were not particularly articulate--roughly on par with his oral argument before the Supreme Court. There was no depth or curiosity conveyed.  I actually think Butler tripped up on Senator Blumenthal's questions about January 6 and the election, but it didn't matter. He sailed through. Members of the conservative legal movement have raised doubts about Butler. But there were no tough questions asked by Senators Cruz, Lee, Hawley, Schmidt, or others. Only they know why they stayed out. Senator Wicker prevailed, and the President lost.

Then there is the bizarre situation in Oklahoma. Someone yesterday asked me if I knew what Senator Armstrong was doing. My response was, "Who is Senator Armstrong?" He is the temporary senator appointed to fill Senator Mullins's seat. As Mike Fragoso relays, Armstrong is blocking the nomination of Zach West to the District Court in Oklahoma. This is all about some sort of squabble between West and defeated-AG Drummond. Armstrong returned a blue slip but is now trying to take it back. That's not how things work. If Armstrong prevails here, the President will lose.

Circuit seats belong to the circuit, and not to the state. It bothers me that "home state" senators introduce circuit court nominees. That pageantry reinforces the wrong message. Hiland's seat does not belong to Arkansas and Butler's seat does not belong to Mississippi.

Unfortunately, Trump's surrender here has created a terrible precedent. Should the Republicans ever again return to power, I would hope this entire process is reconsidered. Circuit court nominees should be treated as "at large" seats. Senators can make recommendations, but they cannot dictate who is picked. Worse, judges (like Southwick) should not be allowed to make these deals. We should not tolerate incentive structure where motivated actors can control who represents an entire circuit. Maybe the better approach is to start consulting with all the Senators in a given circuit on possible picks, and then pick the best athlete.

#7703. What Should You Do With Pumpkins After Halloween?

Should you compost pumpkins after Halloween, toss them in the trash or leave them out for wildlife? Experts explain the options.

Before they migrated to North America, the Irish and Scottish immigrants who established the tradition of jack-o’-lanterns, carved turnips. In the New World, they started carving pumpkins, which were readily available and far more dramatic. Since then, the Halloween tradition they established in the 19th century has only grown more popular and sees more and more pumpkins discarded every year.

How many? “One billion (with a B!),” exclaims composter Lauren Click, and that’s not good, because not everyone responsibly disposes of their jack-o’-lanterns responsibly.

If you care about soil, wildlife and the environment in general, there really is a right way and a wrong way to dispose of pumpkins after Halloween. A gardening expert, a composting expert and a worm farmer explain the difference.

Definitely, yes. “There are many ways to compost a pumpkin,” says Click. “I chop mine up into smaller pieces and feed it to my indoor worm compost farm. You can compost all parts of a pumpkin as long as it is not treated with chemicals, has no paint (so, no painted pumpkins), no glitter, and no plastic/wax/metal candle residue. You can even compost moldy/gross pumpkins!”

It’s important to chop up the pumpkin and not throw it on the compost pile whole, adds UK gardener David Denyer. “Pumpkins decompose slowly if left whole because of their thick rind and high water content. Because of this, adding them straight to your compost can throw off the balance, making the heap turn slimy or even anaerobic, which stops it from breaking down properly.”

One option is to give them to animal rescues and local farmers to use as feed for pigs, chickens and livestock. Click loves this option because, as she says, many farmers compost manure, which makes it a win-win situation. The pumpkin winds up providing nourishment in the soil for more pumpkins.

If you live in the city, worm farmer Scott Kent has another suggestion: “Take your leftover pumpkins is to a worm farm! Composting worms, like red wigglers, consume organic waste and create worm castings from it. Pumpkins, and most all other cucurbits for that matter, are among composting worms’ most favorite foods.”

For a quick way to recycle pumpkins after Halloween that you can do at home, cut the pumpkin into small chunks and bury them in your garden. “This works like a green manure,” says Denyer, “adding organic matter below the surface where it can decompose safely without attracting any pests or spreading disease.”

This is generally a bad idea, say our experts. Click worries about attracting wildlife to areas in which they can be harmed, but beyond that, decomposing pumpkins are not the best source of nutrition. “The acidity and mold that develops as they rot can make hedgehogs, insects, and birds unwell,” says Denyer, who lives where hedgehogs are a thing.

The danger to wildlife increases if the pumpkin contains toxic materials. If you wouldn’t feed, paint, glitter or candle wax to a pet, you shouldn’t feed it to wildlife.

Before carving a pumpkin, most people remove the seeds. Don’t throw them out. When you roast them, they make a delicious snack. After the seeds are gone, the rind makes a good (if temporary) planter for displaying your fall blooms on the porch. Just remember to line the inside to prevent dirt from spilling out from the face you carved.

Composting may be the best way to recycle a pumpkin rind, but if you’re okay with a less dramatic jack-o’-lantern, a smaller pumpkin like a Hokkaido or Baby-Bear can serve a double purpose. Unlike large carving pumpkins with thick, waxy skins, these smaller varieties have thin skins and a high sugar content that make them delicious in soup.

Don’t just toss  them in the garden, warns Denyer: “Pumpkins are high in water and sugars, which means they quickly break down into a thick, slimy layer that blocks air circulation and traps moisture around plant roots. This can then encourage fungal problems, like grey mold or powdery mildew, which can spread to nearby plants.”

It’s important to check with the local waste management rules, because some communities don’t allow pumpkins in yard waste bins. If your community allows them, remove candle wax and other inorganic materials.

Painted pumpkins present a problem: They are organic, but because of the paint, you shouldn’t throw them in organic waste, and some communities prohibit organic materials in the general trash. In such cases, cutting up and burying your pumpkins after Halloween is probably the best solution.

If you leave a whole pumpkin out in the field, it will start decomposing about eight or 12 weeks after it’s fully ripe. Once you cut a pumpkin into smaller pieces and throw them in a compost pile, the pieces will start to rot in five to 10 days.

Full decomposition depends on the moisture content of the air and soil, and on the temperature. It occurs faster when there’s lots of moisture and the air is warm.

Generally, no. Most paints contain toxic chemicals that can poison the compost and the soil on which you spread it. This isn’t necessarily true for all paints, including some water-soluble plant- or egg-based children’s paints, but if you don’t know where the paint came from, keep the painted pumpkin out of the compost.

A paint may be safe for kids, but that doesn’t mean it’s safe for composting. Crayola, a manufacturer of safe-to-use paints for children, recommends using them on pumpkins but warns that those pumpkins should not be consumed (meaning they should not go in the compost).

#7702. Who Is Left On The Bench For 2033?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Even if a Republican wins the 2028 presidential election, it will be virtually impossible for the Senate to flip red during his term. In all likelihood, there will not be a Republican President with a Republican Senate until 2033. As a result, it is unlikely that any conservatives are appointed to the Supreme Court, or the lower courts, over the next six years. A friend suggested, mostly in jest, that Chief Justice Roberts should resign to allow his seat to be filled during divided government. But I suspect the Democrats would just keep the seat open for two, four, even six years.

Ed Whelan writes, "The number of current Trump appellate appointees who will be 55 or younger in 2033 will be 18, and only 6 of those will be 50 or younger." Here is my (approximate) list of judges who Trump circuit appointees who were born after 1977. The six judges in blue at the end are the only ones who would be under 50--none from Trump's first term.

Of course, this all assumes there is no Court "reform" and there will still be a Supreme Court to worry about in six years.

I would make one other observation. Several of the judges who are accused of "auditioning" will likely age out of the Supreme Court short list by 2033. Can we finally exit the audition trap? Let's treat each opinion they write as a reflection of their best judgment, and not some attempt to secure higher office.

When temperatures plummet, heated gloves provide a level of warmth that standard insulation just can’t match. Unlike traditional winter gloves, these everyday essentials generate actual heat to keep hands cozy in extreme cold. Most rely on rechargeable batteries to power internal wiring, though some use chemical heat packs or microwave heating.

We included each of these tested sets of heated gloves for their ability to stay warm and provide comfortable functionality. Depending on your needs, at least one pair should be right for you.

Featuring a polyester and elastane exterior with leather palms, these Savior gloves provide a flexible, reliable grip for winter tasks. Their polyurethane lining and 3M Thinsulate insulation were soft and relatively warm—even without the heating element. Then, once we switched on the heat, we felt a noticeable warmth spread across the backs of our hands and fingers. In addition to being powerful, the slim lithium-ion batteries were barely noticeable in their zippered wrist pouches.

With three heat settings, these gloves can generate warmth for up to 7 hours. We found them comfortable, appreciated their touch-screen compatibility, and were impressed by their water resistance. After dousing them with water to simulate wet winter weather, the interiors remained completely dry throughout a full day of testing.

Get the Savior battery-heated gloves at Amazon.

If you’re after a balance of warmth and dexterity for everyday use, these YongGfte heated fingerless gloves might be perfect. The half-finger design with magnetic mitten covers is great for walking the dog or performing basic outdoor tasks that require occasional fingertip access. As a non-insulated, non-weather-resistant option, they’re better for moderately cold and dry weather than extreme temperatures or precipitation.

During testing, we liked having heat on both our palms and the backs of our hands, though our fingers and thumbs noticed its absence when in the wind. As advertised, we got almost 4 hours of warmth during use on low, but on high, the battery only lasted about an hour. Also, the rechargeable batteries are fully integrated rather than removable, so there’s no way to wear the gloves while the batteries charge. Given their reasonable price, however, they’re an excellent choice if you don’t want to fuss with something big and bulky on not-super-cold days.

These Snow Deer heated glove liners are ideal for anyone who already has good gloves but wants an extra boost on especially cold days. On their own, we found them sufficient for keeping our hands warm in cool weather, as they offer slightly more wind protection than plain fleece. The flexible exterior and thin, insulated interior can also be worn inside waterproof outer gloves, size permitting, for wet or snowy conditions.

The heating wires on these thermal heated gloves extend across the entire back of the hand to the fingertips, and the heat is easy to control via a push button on each wrist cuff. The rechargeable lithium-ion batteries fit in zippered pouches on the inside wrist cuff and run for close to 7 hours. Get the Snow Deer rechargeable heated gloves at Amazon.

Wasoto’s heated leather gloves combine the best of both worlds for outdoor work: consistent heat and rugged functionality. We could tell these Savior gloves were rugged right out of the package. They feature carbon fiber knuckle guards for increased protection when riding a motorcycle or snowmobile and reinforced padded leather palms to reduce fatigue when gripping handlebars. Whether you’re inching down bunny slopes or tackling black-diamond runs, these Snow Deer heated ski gloves are designed for serious warmth.
